Markus Gesmann and Jake Morris, *Hierarchical Compartmental Reserving
Models* (CAS Research Paper, 2020), model a reserve as quantities that flow
between compartments at rates. A pharmacologist models a drug in the body in
the same way. Claims arise from premium. They stay in outstanding while they
are known but unpaid, and they move to paid when they settle. One small set of
parameters, each with a business meaning, describes the paid triangle and the
outstanding triangle together.

This guide explains the idea and fits the paper's two models to its example
company with prospicio (`compartmental()`). It compares prospicio's posterior
summaries with the paper's printed summaries.

This is the R twin of the Python guide
[`reserving-compartmental.md`](reserving-compartmental.md). It has the same
sections, models, checks and recorded numbers. It uses the R package
functions `gesmann_morris_priors()`, `gesmann_morris_2_priors()`,
`compartmental_prior_predictive()`, `compartmental()`,
`compartmental_model_2()`, `bayes_loo()`, `compartmental_one_year()` and
`compartmental_model_2_one_year()`. The R package calls the same Rust code as
the Python package.

The paper's text is the authors'. Read the paper for the derivations. The
paper fits its models with the R package brms, which writes a Stan program.
prospicio samples the same posterior with its own NUTS sampler. Money is in
thousands of US dollars, as in the data. For a general choice of reserving
method, read [`reserving-methods.md`](reserving-methods.md). For Meyers'
Bayesian models on one triangle, read [`reserving-meyers.md`](reserving-meyers.md).

**How the numbers here are checked.** CI (`R/prospicio/tests/test-guides.R`)
runs each R chunk that has a text block after it, and the chunk must print
exactly that text. This text is the same as in the Python guide, except for
one line in section 7. To render the page, install the R package and run
`quarto render docs/guides/reserving-compartmental.qmd`.

Model 1 runs in CI with prospicio's default sampler: 4 chains of 1,000 warm-up
draws and 2,000 kept draws. It takes about 5 to 9 seconds in a release build
(about 12 seconds in R on Windows). A model 2 fit takes about a minute and a
one-year view takes several minutes, so CI does not run them. Three points
apply to every comparison:

* A Bayesian result is a Monte Carlo estimate. Another seed gives a slightly
  different number, and the paper's own run has the same error. Each
  comparison states how far a number moves from seed to seed. These amounts
  come from the 200-seed studies in
  `knowledge/findings/compartmental-gm1-parity.md` and
  `compartmental-gm2-parity.md` (CI does not run these studies).
* The exact digits of a NUTS run depend on the platform. The last bit of `exp`
  and `ln` differs between Windows and Linux, so the sampler's paths diverge
  and the draws differ. Thus each checked chunk prints the paper's value, a
  tolerance a few Monte Carlo errors wide, and whether prospicio's value is in
  the tolerance. Where the paper prints no value, the chunk uses the paper's
  code, run again in Stan. prospicio's own values are in plain `r` blocks,
  with numbers from one run of the Python guide (Windows x86_64, release
  build, seed 0). **CI does not run
  these blocks, which include every model 2 fit and both one-year views.**
* On Windows, the R package is built with the GNU toolchain. Its `exp` and
  `ln` differ again in the last bit from the MSVC build of the Python package,
  so its seed-0 draws also differ. For example, the `b_ker` mean of model 1 is
  -5.388 against -5.395 in Python, and its total reserve mean is 173,584
  against 173,457. Every checked chunk prints the same text. The prior
  predictive check has no sampler paths, so it prints the same digits as
  Python.

## 1. The compartmental idea

Think of three tanks. The first tank, exposure (EX), starts each accident year
full with the expected losses of that year. Claims leave it when they are
reported, at a rate `k_er` a year, and go into the second tank, outstanding
(OS). Claims leave outstanding when they are settled, at a rate `k_p` a year,
and go into the third tank, paid (PD).

Linear differential equations describe the flow. With constant rates, they
have a closed form. Let `t` be the development time in years (12 months is
`t = 1`) and let

    g(t) = (exp(-k_p t) - exp(-k_er t)) / (k_er - k_p)

Then the expected outstanding and cumulative paid of origin `i` with premium
`P_i` are

    OS_i(t) = P_i RLR_i k_er g(t)
    PD_i(t) = P_i RLR_i RRF_i [(1 - exp(-k_p t)) - k_p g(t)]

Outstanding rises from zero to a peak and then decreases. Paid rises toward
its ultimate. Each of the four parameters describes the business:

* `RLR_i`, the reported loss ratio: the share of premium that goes through
  outstanding, valued at the level of the case reserves.
* `RRF_i`, the reserve robustness factor: the part of the reported amount
  that is paid in the end. Below 1, the case reserves are redundant. Above 1,
  they are not sufficient.
* `RLR_i RRF_i`, the ultimate loss ratio. It has the role of the expected loss
  ratio (ELR) in a Bornhuetter-Ferguson or Cape Cod reserve. But the model
  estimates it from paid and outstanding together, and it is not a separate
  selection.
* `k_er` and `k_p`, the speeds of reporting and payment. In model 1, all
  accident years share them. In model 2, they vary by accident year and
  development year.

**The hierarchy.** `RLR` and `RRF` vary by accident year, but not freely. The
value of each year is the population value times a random effect. The two
effects are correlated, and the model estimates their spread from the data. A
young year with little data uses information from the other years, as a
credibility-weighted ELR does. A mature year depends mostly on its own data.
An accident year with premium and no data (1997 below) takes a new effect from
the population in each simulation.

**Identification.** The two rates can change places, with `RLR` and `RRF`
rescaled, and every mean stays exactly the same
(`knowledge/findings/compartmental-rate-swap.md`). Only the priors separate
the two mirror solutions. prospicio gives a warning if a posterior draw has
`k_er <= k_p`. No draw does here.

## 2. Company 337

The paper uses NAIC company 337, workers' compensation, accident years 1988 to
1997, from the CAS loss reserve database. Its outstanding is incurred (with
bulk and IBNR reserves) less paid. Its premium is direct earned premium. The
training data are the calendar years up to 1996. They contain 45 paid cells
and 45 outstanding cells for 1988 to 1996, and the premium of 1997 only. The
data hold the full 10 by 10 square, so the 1997 calendar diagonal and the
120-month outcome are known and test the forecast.

```{r}
library(prospicio)

# The data file, found from the repository root (CI) or from docs/guides (Quarto).
find_data <- function(name, dir = getwd()) {
  repeat {
    path <- file.path(dir, "validation", "data", name)
    if (file.exists(path)) return(path)
    parent <- dirname(dir)
    if (identical(parent, dir)) stop("validation/data/", name, " not found", call. = FALSE)
    dir <- parent
  }
}

# Python's format specs: ",.0f" (thousands), ".1f", ".2f", ".3f", ".4f".
fmt <- function(x, spec = ",.0f", width = 0) {
  out <- switch(spec,
    ",.0f" = formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 0, big.mark = ","),
    ".1f" = sprintf("%.1f", x),
    ".2f" = sprintf("%.2f", x),
    ".3f" = sprintf("%.3f", x),
    ".4f" = sprintf("%.4f", x))
  formatC(out, width = width)
}
# numpy's std: the population standard deviation.
psd <- function(x) sqrt(mean((x - mean(x))^2))

square <- utils::read.csv(find_data("clrd_wkcomp_337.csv"), comment.char = "#")
square$os <- square$incurred - square$paid
cell <- function(origin, age, key) square[[key]][square$origin == origin & square$development == age]
premium <- stats::setNames(square$premium[square$development == 12],
                           square$origin[square$development == 12])

# Training cells: calendar years up to 1996. 1997 enters with its premium only.
cols <- c("origin", "development", "paid", "incurred", "premium")
train <- square[square$origin + square$development %/% 12 - 1 <= 1996, cols]
y1997 <- square[square$origin == 1997 & square$development == 12, cols]
y1997$paid <- NA
y1997$incurred <- NA
tri <- triangle(rbind(train, y1997), "origin", "development", c("paid", "incurred", "premium"))
latest_paid <- sum(train$paid[train$origin + train$development %/% 12 - 1 == 1996])
ultimate_paid <- sum(square$paid[square$development == 120])
cat(sprintf("training cells %d of each type, premium %s\n", nrow(train), fmt(sum(premium))))
cat(sprintf("1988 at 12 months: premium %s, paid %s, outstanding %s\n", fmt(premium[["1988"]]),
            fmt(cell(1988, 12, "paid")), fmt(cell(1988, 12, "os"))))
cat(sprintf("latest paid %s; paid at 120 months %s; outcome reserve %s\n", fmt(latest_paid),
            fmt(ultimate_paid), fmt(ultimate_paid - latest_paid)))
```

```text
training cells 45 of each type, premium 903,152
1988 at 12 months: premium 104,437, paid 9,558, outstanding 53,121
latest paid 402,015; paid at 120 months 589,435; outcome reserve 187,420
```

Morris (2016), the predecessor of the paper, printed the same 1988 cell in
millions: premium 104, outstanding 53, paid 10. The outcome reserve is the
amount that every accident year, 1997 included, paid after the end of 1996 up
to 120 months. The models below try to predict this number.

## 3. Priors, and the prior predictive check

The priors are a required argument of `compartmental()`, because the rates and loss
ratios are specific to a line and a book. `gesmann_morris_priors()` is the paper's set for
model 1. Each positive parameter is a median times `exp(sd o)`, with `o`
standard normal. The medians are `k_er` 3 (sd 0.1 on the log scale), `k_p` 1
(0.1), `RLR` 0.7 (0.2) and `RRF` 0.8 (0.1). The sds of the accident-year
effects have half Student-t priors (scales 0.2 and 0.1 on that `o` scale).
Their correlation has a uniform LKJ(1) prior, and each `log sigma` has a
Student-t prior so wide that it is effectively flat.

The paper recommends a prior predictive check before the fit. Draw the
parameters from the priors alone, calculate the curves, and examine whether
the development looks like a plausible book. `compartmental_prior_predictive()` returns those paths (the
means, without the noise of the likelihood). The block below prints the paid
and outstanding loss ratios of 1988 under the priors, and the actual values of
1988:

```{r}
gm1 <- gesmann_morris_priors()


# `...` passes model 2's paid response, incremental: each year's paid uses that
# year's development effects.
prior_check <- function(priors, label, ...) {
  paths <- compartmental_prior_predictive(tri, "premium", priors, n_sims = 2000, ...)
  cat(sprintf("%s: 1988 loss ratios under the priors alone (5%%, 50%%, 95%%) and actual\n", label))
  for (kind in c("paid", "outstanding")) {
    key <- if (kind == "paid") "paid" else "os"
    for (age in c(12, 36, 120)) {
      m <- marginal(paths[[kind]], list(origin = "1988", age = age))
      q <- quantile(m, c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95)) / premium[["1988"]]
      actual <- cell(1988, age, key) / premium[["1988"]]
      cat(sprintf("  %-11s %3d months  %.2f %.2f %.2f   actual %.2f\n", kind, age, q[1], q[2], q[3],
                  actual))
    }
  }
}


prior_check(gm1, "model 1")
```

```text
model 1: 1988 loss ratios under the priors alone (5%, 50%, 95%) and actual
  paid         12 months  0.18 0.26 0.39   actual 0.09
  paid         36 months  0.36 0.52 0.76   actual 0.32
  paid        120 months  0.39 0.56 0.82   actual 0.50
  outstanding  12 months  0.24 0.33 0.47   actual 0.51
  outstanding  36 months  0.03 0.05 0.09   actual 0.31
  outstanding 120 months  0.00 0.00 0.00   actual 0.01
```

The check finds a conflict before the fit. Under the preset, payment is fast
(`k_p` near 1 a year). Thus the priors put about a quarter of premium in paid
after 12 months, and outstanding is empty within a few years. Company 337 pays
much more slowly: 9% paid at 12 months, and 31% of premium outstanding at 36
months, where the priors expect about 5%. The data move the rates many prior
sds away (section 4: `k_er` about 1.76 and `k_p` about 0.43, against medians 3
and 1).

The paper keeps the preset. For your own book, make the rate priors wider or
move their centre after a check like this one.
For example, build a set with `compartmental_priors()`.

## 4. Model 1: one likelihood for paid and outstanding amounts

Model 1 puts a normal likelihood on each observed cumulative paid amount and
outstanding amount, centred on its curve, with one `sigma` for each type.
`RLR` and `RRF` vary by accident year, and the rates do not. The paper prints
its posterior summary (`m1fit`, section 7.2.2) on the brms scale. The summary
gives the intercepts `b_*` on the standardised `o` scale of each parameter,
and the sds `tau` of the accident-year effects on that scale. It also gives
their correlation `rho` and the `log sigma` of each type. prospicio reports
the same names.

prospicio's means move by at most 0.032 posterior sds from seed to seed, and
its sds by at most 2.3% (200 seeds). The paper's run had about 1,300 to 2,200
effective draws, so its means also have about 0.03 sds of error. The paper
rounds to two decimals. A tolerance of 0.15 printed sds plus 0.005 (for the
rounding) on a mean, and 10% on an sd, is about three combined errors wide.

```{r}
check <- function(label, target, ours, tol, spec = ".3f", source = "paper") {
  agrees <- abs(ours - target) <= tol
  cat(sprintf("%-24s %-5s %9s  tolerance %7s  agrees: %s\n", label, source, fmt(target, spec),
              fmt(tol, spec), if (agrees) "True" else "False"))
  invisible(agrees)
}


# The fit and how many warnings it raised.
fit_quietly <- function(expr) {
  n <- 0
  fit <- withCallingHandlers(expr, warning = function(w) {
    n <<- n + 1
    invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
  })
  list(fit = fit, n_warnings = n)
}


param <- function(fit, name, column = "mean") {
  s <- fit@summary
  s[[column]][s$parameter == name]
}


check_posterior <- function(fit, printed) {
  ok <- 0
  for (name in names(printed)) {
    mean <- printed[[name]][1]
    sd <- printed[[name]][2]
    ok <- ok + check(paste(name, "mean"), mean, param(fit, name), 0.15 * sd + 0.005, ".4f")
    ok <- ok + check(paste(name, "sd"), sd, param(fit, name, "sd"), 0.10 * sd + 0.005, ".4f")
  }
  ok
}


# The paper's printed m1fit, mean and sd.
M1FIT <- list(
  b_ker = c(-5.40, 0.81), b_kp = c(-8.49, 0.36), b_RLR = c(1.44, 0.26), b_RRF = c(-1.36, 0.42),
  tau_RLR = c(0.64, 0.15), tau_RRF = c(0.74, 0.22), rho = c(0.54, 0.26),
  log_sigma_os = c(8.25, 0.16), log_sigma_pd = c(6.66, 0.20)
)
run1 <- fit_quietly(compartmental(tri, "paid", "premium", gm1, incurred = "incurred",
                                  n_sims = 2000))
fit1 <- run1$fit
cat(sprintf("warnings %d | rate swaps %d\n", run1$n_warnings, fit1@rate_swaps))
cat(sprintf("rows agreeing %d of %d\n", check_posterior(fit1, M1FIT), 2 * length(M1FIT)))
```

```text
warnings 0 | rate swaps 0

b_ker sd                 paper    0.8100  tolerance  0.0860  agrees: True
```

Every row agrees. On Windows at seed 0, prospicio gives these posterior means
(sds in parentheses):

| Parameter | Mean (sd) | Parameter | Mean (sd) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `b_ker` | -5.395 (0.833) | `tau_RRF` | 0.739 (0.220) |
| `b_kp` | -8.485 (0.356) | `rho` | 0.533 (0.259) |

| `tau_RLR` | 0.643 (0.150) | | |

The largest difference from the paper is 0.011 on `log_sigma_pd`, which is
0.055 printed sds. A reconstruction of the brms Stan program, run under
CmdStan for 100,000 draws, gives values within 0.04 sds of the paper
(`knowledge/references/gesmann-morris-2020.md`).

On the natural scale, `k_er` is about 1.76 and `k_p` about 0.43 a year. On
average, claims are reported about seven months after the start (`1 / k_er`
years) and paid about 2.3 years after that (`1 / k_p`). The population `RLR`
is about 0.94 and `RRF` about 0.70. Thus the case reserves (with bulk) are
redundant by about 30%, and the population ultimate loss ratio is about 0.65:

```r
for (name in c("k_er", "k_p", "RLR", "RRF")) {
  cat(sprintf("%-4s posterior mean %.2f, 90%% interval %.2f to %.2f\n", name, param(fit1, name),
              param(fit1, name, "q05"), param(fit1, name, "q95")))
}
```

```text

k_p  posterior mean 0.43, 90% interval 0.40 to 0.45
RLR  posterior mean 0.94, 90% interval 0.86 to 1.02
RRF  posterior mean 0.70, 90% interval 0.65 to 0.75
```

## 5. The fitted paid and outstanding development

Each posterior draw gives a curve from its rates and from the `RLR` and `RRF`
of its accident year. The fit is the posterior mean of these curves. The block
below shows a mature accident year and a young one, with the actual and fitted
values at each observed age:

```r
par <- fit1@draws


fitted <- function(origin, age) {
  ker <- par[, "k_er"]
  kp <- par[, "k_p"]
  rlr <- par[, sprintf("RLR[%d]", origin)]
  rrf <- par[, sprintf("RRF[%d]", origin)]
  t <- age / 12
  g <- (exp(-kp * t) - exp(-ker * t)) / (ker - kp)
  p <- premium[[as.character(origin)]]
  c(os = mean(p * rlr * ker * g), pd = mean(p * rlr * rrf * ((1 - exp(-kp * t)) - kp * g)))
}


for (origin in c(1988, 1994)) {
  cat(sprintf("%d  age   paid actual  fitted   outstanding actual  fitted\n", origin))
  for (age in seq(12, 12 * (1997 - origin), by = 12)) {
    f <- fitted(origin, age)
    cat(sprintf("      %3d  %11s %7s  %18s %7s\n", age, fmt(cell(origin, age, "paid")), fmt(f[["pd"]]),
                fmt(cell(origin, age, "os")), fmt(f[["os"]])))
  }
}
```

```text

       24       22,778  23,740              41,222  43,904
       36       33,298  33,712              32,309  30,258
       48       40,348  40,423              24,944  20,017
       60       45,146  44,835              17,104  13,101
       72       48,048  47,718              13,137   8,551
       84       49,782  49,599               9,605   5,578
       96       50,623  50,826               6,515   3,638
      108       51,812  51,626               1,661   2,373
```

Paid fits closely at every age. Outstanding does not. The actual outstanding
of 1988 decreases more slowly than the two-rate curve permits. It is 24,944
at 48 months against 20,017 fitted, and 13,137 at 72 months against 8,551. The curve
compensates at the latest age. With one `k_p` for every age, only slower
payment can keep outstanding high for longer, and the paid cells do not agree
with slower payment.

A normal likelihood with one `sigma` for each type also measures the error of
a cell in absolute terms. Thus the large early cells dominate, and the small
late cells fit loosely. Model 2 (section 7) addresses both points.

The test diagonal, calendar year 1997, is not in the training data. The
`paid` and `outstanding` of the fit are the posterior predictive distributions
of every future cell, with the noise of the likelihood:

```r
cat("origin age   paid actual  predicted (5% to 95%)      outstanding actual  predicted (5% to 95%)\n")
inside <- 0
for (origin in 1988:1997) {
  age <- 12 * (1997 - origin + 1)
  row <- sprintf("%d  %3d", origin, age)
  for (kind in c("paid", "outstanding")) {
    dist <- if (kind == "paid") fit1@paid else fit1@outstanding
    m <- marginal(dist, list(origin = as.character(origin), age = age))
    q <- quantile(m, c(0.05, 0.95))
    actual <- cell(origin, age, if (kind == "paid") "paid" else "os")
    inside <- inside + (q[[1]] <= actual && actual <= q[[2]])
    row <- paste0(row, sprintf("  %11s %9s (%7s to %7s)", fmt(actual), fmt(mean(m)), fmt(q[[1]]),
                               fmt(q[[2]])))
  }
  cat(row, "\n", sep = "")
}
cat(sprintf("actual inside the 90%% interval: %d of 20 cells\n", inside))
```


Seventeen of the twenty cells are inside their 90% intervals. Two of the three
misses are in the youngest accident year. The first paid (9,372) and
outstanding (40,799) of 1997 are much higher than the model expects from its
premium. This is a first sign of the result that section 7 finds in the
reserve.

The outstanding intervals of the old years go below zero. The normal
likelihood with a constant `sigma` (about 3,900) does not use the size of a
cell. This is another reason for the log-normal likelihood of model 2.

## 6. The reserve distribution

The reserve of an accident year is its paid at 120 months less its latest
paid. For 1997, the reserve is all of its paid. `fit1@reserves` is the joint
posterior predictive distribution by accident year, with parameter error and
process error.

The paper prints no reserve. Thus the comparison is with the Stan
reconstruction of the paper's code (100,000 draws). At 10,000 simulations,
prospicio's mean moves by about 0.016 sds from seed to seed and its sd by
about 1.4%. These blocks use 2,000 simulations, so the tolerances are 0.1 sds
and 7%:

```{r}
r1 <- draw_matrix(fit1@reserves)
total1 <- rowSums(r1)
check("total reserve mean", 173341, mean(total1), 1000, ",.0f", "Stan")
check("total reserve sd", 10076, psd(total1), 700, ",.0f", "Stan")
i97 <- which(fit1@origins == "1997")
check("1997 reserve mean", 31321, mean(r1[, i97]), 600, ",.0f", "Stan")
check("1997 reserve sd", 6125, psd(r1[, i97]), 430, ",.0f", "Stan")
outcome <- ultimate_paid - latest_paid
q <- quantile(total1, c(0.05, 0.95), names = FALSE)
cat(sprintf("outcome %s inside the 90%% interval: %s\n", fmt(outcome),
            if (q[1] <= outcome && outcome <= q[2]) "True" else "False"))
```

The total reserve is about 173,500 with an sd of about 10,300 (Stan's

## 7. Model 2: log-normal loss ratios and effects on the rates

Model 2 changes three things:

* **The response.** Model 2 models loss ratios to premium, not amounts. For
  paid, it uses the incremental paid loss ratio of each year, not the
  cumulative one. An incremental cell is the difference of the paid curve
  between `t - 1` and `t`. Cumulative paid cells are strongly correlated, and
  an independent likelihood on them overstates their information. Incremental
  cells are closer to independent.
* **The likelihood.** Each response is log-normal about its curve, so the
  noise is proportional to the size of the cell. Thus a large early cell does
  not swamp a small late cell, as it does under the constant `sigma` of model
  1. The `log sigma` priors are now informative: normal, with median 0.2 for
  `sigma`. This is the value in the paper's code. The paper's text gives 0.1
  (see the reference note).
* **The hierarchy.** All four parameters have accident-year effects (`RLR` and
  `RRF` correlated, the rates independent). All four also have
  development-year effects, so each cell has its own `k_er`, `k_p`, `RLR` and
  `RRF`. A development effect lets the curve bend where the two-rate shape is
  too stiff. An age with no observed cell (120 months here) draws a new effect
  from the population.

`compartmental_model_2()` with `gesmann_morris_2_priors()` fits model 2. It has a longer sampler than model 1: 4 chains of 2,000 warm-up
draws and 8,000 kept draws, at target acceptance 0.999. The model has 87
parameters, several effect sds near zero and a slowly mixing `k_p`. With the
sampler of model 1, it gave divergent transitions on most seeds. Its prior
predictive check is fast, so it runs. The Python chunk also prints the settings of the model in its first line:

```{r}
gm2 <- gesmann_morris_2_priors()
prior_check(gm2, "model 2", paid_response = "incremental")
```

```text
model 2: 1988 loss ratios under the priors alone (5%, 50%, 95%) and actual
  paid         12 months  0.15 0.26 0.45   actual 0.09
  paid         36 months  0.32 0.51 0.85   actual 0.32
  paid        120 months  0.35 0.56 0.92   actual 0.50
  outstanding  12 months  0.20 0.33 0.57   actual 0.51
  outstanding  36 months  0.03 0.05 0.10   actual 0.31
  outstanding 120 months  0.00 0.00 0.00   actual 0.01
```

The medians are the same as for model 1, because the rate priors and ratio
priors are the same. The intervals are wider, because each development year
and accident year can also shift the rates and ratios. The conflict with the
slow payment of company 337 is the same. The posterior again moves far from
the preset, but less than for model 1, because the development effects can
now bend the curve. At the population, `k_er` is about 2.6 and `k_p` about
0.60, against 1.76 and 0.43 for model 1.

The fit takes about a minute. The block below compares it with the paper's
printed `m2fit` (section 7.2.3). It shows prospicio's value and the difference
in printed sds:

```r
M2FIT <- list(
  b_ker = c(-1.31, 1.08), b_kp = c(-5.07, 1.75), b_RLR = c(1.54, 0.44), b_RRF = c(-1.45, 0.69),
  tau_RLR = c(0.69, 0.31), tau_RRF = c(0.73, 0.47), tau_ker = c(0.26, 0.22),
  tau_kp = c(2.23, 1.35), rho = c(0.37, 0.47), tau_dev_RLR = c(0.35, 0.26),
  tau_dev_RRF = c(1.11, 0.49), tau_dev_ker = c(0.27, 0.23), tau_dev_kp = c(0.45, 0.43),
  log_sigma_os = c(-1.78, 0.16), log_sigma_pd = c(-1.89, 0.16)
)
run2 <- fit_quietly(compartmental_model_2(tri, "paid", "premium", gm2, incurred = "incurred",
                                          n_sims = 2000))
fit2 <- run2$fit
cat(sprintf("warnings %d | draws with k_er <= k_p in an observed cell %.1f\n", run2$n_warnings,
            fit2@cell_rate_swaps))
cat(sprintf("%-14s %10s %7s %7s   %8s %6s\n", "", "paper mean", "ours", "gap/sd", "paper sd", "ours"))
for (name in names(M2FIT)) {
  mean <- M2FIT[[name]][1]
  sd <- M2FIT[[name]][2]
  m <- param(fit2, name)
  cat(sprintf("%-14s %10.2f %7.3f %7.3f   %8.2f %6.3f\n", name, mean, m, (m - mean) / sd, sd,
              param(fit2, name, "sd")))
}
```

Every mean is within 0.08 printed sds of the paper's mean. Every sd is within
4% of the paper's sd, except `tau_dev_kp`, the sd of the development effects
on `k_p`: 0.511 against the printed 0.43. This sd has a heavy tail and mixes
slowly. The paper's own run had only about 500 effective draws on the
parameters of `k_p`. The Stan reconstruction of the paper's code with 100,000
draws gives 0.518. Thus the difference is the paper's Monte Carlo error, not
a difference of model.

prospicio's means move by at most 0.036 posterior sds from seed to seed (200
seeds). Every draw keeps `k_er` above `k_p` in every observed cell.

The block below gives the reserves and ultimate loss ratios of the two models,
and the paid of each accident year at 120 months:

```r
r2 <- draw_matrix(fit2@reserves)
total2 <- rowSums(r2)
for (label in c("model 1", "model 2")) {
  t <- if (label == "model 1") total1 else total2
  q <- quantile(t, c(0.05, 0.95), names = FALSE)
  cat(sprintf("%s: total reserve mean %s, sd %s, 5%% %s, 95%% %s; outcome at percentile %.1f\n",
              label, fmt(mean(t)), fmt(psd(t)), fmt(q[1]), fmt(q[2]), 100 * mean(t <= outcome)))
}
cat("ultimate loss ratio by accident year, model 1 and model 2\n")
for (i in seq_along(fit1@origins)) {
  o <- fit1@origins[i]
  actual <- cell(as.integer(o), 120, "paid") / premium[[o]]
  cat(sprintf("  %s  %.3f  %.3f   paid at 120 months %.3f\n", o, fit1@ultimate_loss_ratio[i],
              fit2@ultimate_loss_ratio[i], actual))
}
```

```text
model 2: total reserve mean 151,861, sd 13,729, 5% 130,835, 95% 175,476; outcome at percentile 99.2
ultimate loss ratio by accident year, model 1 and model 2
  1988  0.509  0.543   paid at 120 months 0.497
  1989  0.538  0.582   paid at 120 months 0.523
  1990  0.656  0.686   paid at 120 months 0.638
  1991  0.736  0.727   paid at 120 months 0.694
  1992  0.633  0.657   paid at 120 months 0.604
  1993  0.512  0.565   paid at 120 months 0.485
  1994  0.546  0.586   paid at 120 months 0.499
```

The total of model 2 is about 151,900 (Stan's reconstruction: 152,242, sd
13,938). This is about 21,600 below model 1, with a wider spread. The outcome,
187,420, is at the 92nd percentile of model 1 and the 99th percentile of model
2.

The miss is in the youngest years. 1996 and 1997 paid 1.07 and 1.15 of their
premium by 120 months. Their ultimate loss ratios are 0.89 and 0.67 under
model 2, and 1.04 and 0.67 under model 1. Premium decreased from 119,427 in
1993 to 48,052 in 1997, but losses did not, which is the pattern of a
softening market. Both models shrink a young year toward the population loss
ratio. Model 2 has more effects that share information, so it shrinks more.

One triangle gives one outcome. Thus this result does not show the calibration
of the models in general. It shows only that the shrinkage of young years
needs a judgement when the market changes.

## 8. Do not compare the two models by elpd_loo

Both fits report PSIS-LOO (`bayes_loo()`): the expected log predictive density of
each observed cell, with that cell left out. Do not compare the elpd_loo of
model 1 with that of model 2. The responses of model 1 are amounts in
thousands, with cumulative paid. The responses of model 2 are loss ratios,
with incremental paid. A log density depends on the unit of its response.
Thus the two numbers are on different scales and do not show which model
predicts better.

Compare elpd_loo only between fits of the same responses, for example two
prior sets for model 1. CI runs the elpd_loo of model 1 and checks it against
the Stan reconstruction, which moves by about 0.35 from seed to seed:

```{r}
loo1 <- bayes_loo(fit1)
check("model 1 elpd_loo", -811.0, loo1$estimates[["elpd"]], 2.0, ".1f", "Stan")
cat(sprintf("model 1 cells with Pareto k above 0.7: at least one %s\n",
            if (any(loo1$pareto_k > 0.7)) "True" else "False"))
```

```text
model 1 elpd_loo         Stan     -811.0  tolerance     2.0  agrees: True
model 1 cells with Pareto k above 0.7: at least one True
```

```r
for (label in c("model 1", "model 2")) {
  loo <- bayes_loo(if (label == "model 1") fit1 else fit2)
  k <- loo$pareto_k
  cat(sprintf(paste0("%s: elpd_loo %.1f (se %.1f), outstanding %.1f, paid %.1f; ",
                     "Pareto k above 0.7 in %d of %d cells, largest %.2f\n"),
              label, loo$estimates[["elpd"]], loo$estimates[["se"]], loo$elpd_outstanding,
              loo$elpd_paid, sum(k > 0.7), length(k), max(k)))
}
```

```text
model 1: elpd_loo -810.7 (se 10.2), outstanding -440.8, paid -370.0; Pareto k above 0.7 in 3 of 90 cells, largest 0.96
model 2: elpd_loo 203.8 (se 11.5), outstanding 71.5, paid 132.2; Pareto k above 0.7 in 9 of 90 cells, largest 1.30
```

A few cells have Pareto `k` above 0.7. In these cells, the importance sampling
approximation behind PSIS-LOO is not reliable. The left-out cell moves the
posterior too much, so the draws of the full posterior do not represent the
fit without that cell. The elpd_loo is then an estimate with an unknown error,
not a measure of predictive accuracy. Exact LOO, a refit without those cells,
removes this uncertainty.

For model 2, the elpd_loo agreed with the arviz calculation on the same draws
(finding `compartmental-gm2-parity.md`). Thus that row checks the arithmetic,
not the fit. To select between the two models, compare their forecasts of the
test diagonal and of the outcome (sections 5 to 7). These forecasts are on
the same scale.

## 9. The one-year view

A solvency view asks how far the best estimate can move in the next year. It
does not ask how far the reserve can move over its full life. This movement is the claims
development result (CDR): the opening reserve, less the paid of the year, less
the reserve estimated again one year later.

`compartmental_one_year()` simulates the next calendar diagonal (paid and outstanding of every
accident year) from the posterior. For each simulated year, it estimates the
posterior again without a refit. It reweights the existing draws by the
likelihood of the new cells (Pareto smoothed importance sampling).

The new cells move this posterior a lot, so the weights of most simulations
fail the Pareto `k` test (`k` above 0.7). For model 1, prospicio then moment
matches the draws: it applies small affine shifts to the draws so that the
weights are reliable again. It refits with NUTS only the few simulations that
matching cannot rescue. On company 337, matching rescues about 95% of them,
within about 0.05 sds of a refit (`knowledge/findings/compartmental-one-year.md`).
By default, the view runs at most 2,000 simulations and takes several minutes:

```r
run <- fit_quietly(compartmental_one_year(tri, "paid", "premium", gm1, incurred = "incurred",
                                          n_sims = 2000))
view1 <- run$fit
cdr1 <- rowSums(draw_matrix(view1@cdr))
cat(sprintf("model 1: flagged %.0f%%, moment-matched %s, refitted %s, refits with a diagnostic warning %d\n",
            100 * view1@flagged_share, fmt(length(view1@moment_matched)),
            fmt(length(view1@refitted)), view1@refit_warnings))
cat("warnings", run$n_warnings, "\n")
cat(sprintf("total CDR mean %s, sd %s; lifetime reserve sd %s; ratio %.2f\n", fmt(mean(cdr1)),
            fmt(psd(cdr1)), fmt(psd(total1)), psd(cdr1) / psd(total1)))
```

```text
model 1: flagged 81%, moment-matched 1,549, refitted 78, refits with a diagnostic warning 8
warnings 1
total CDR mean 55, sd 7,982; lifetime reserve sd 10,260; ratio 0.78
```

About four in five simulations are flagged. Matching rescues about 95% of
them, and NUTS refits the others, which takes most of the run time. The
warning is about the refits: 8 of them missed an MCMC diagnostic threshold.
Thus read `view1@refit_warnings` before you use the far tail of the CDR. About 78% of the
sd of the lifetime reserve emerges in the first year, which agrees with the
200-seed study (0.80, sd 0.03). The mean of the CDR is about zero, as
expected.

The R package's own run on Windows (seed 0, GNU toolchain) gives
82% flagged, 1,548 matched, 102 refitted and a ratio of 0.81.

For model 2, matching rescues none of the flagged simulations. Its posterior
has 95 sampled values and several effect sds near zero, which is far from the
near-normal shape that the shifts can follow. A refit takes as long as a fit,
so a view with a full refit for each flagged simulation would take days. Thus
the default view refits the flagged simulations with a light refit: a
shorter, warm-started NUTS run, scaled by the opening posterior (`compartmental_model_2_one_year()`). On
company 337, this view is within about 0.03 sds of the total CDR of full
refits. It takes about half an hour at the default 2,000 simulations.

`light_refit = FALSE` reweights only, and gives a warning that the view is approximate.
Such a view is about 0.4 sds of the total CDR from a refit for each
simulation. `one_year_sims`, `refit` and `max_refits` change the balance between
accuracy and time. To save time, the run below reweights only.

```r
run <- fit_quietly(compartmental_model_2_one_year(tri, "paid", "premium", gm2,
                                                  incurred = "incurred", n_sims = 2000,
                                                  light_refit = FALSE))
view2 <- run$fit
cdr2 <- rowSums(draw_matrix(view2@cdr))
cat(sprintf("model 2: flagged %.0f%%, moment-matched %s, refitted %s\n", 100 * view2@flagged_share,
            fmt(length(view2@moment_matched)), fmt(length(view2@refitted))))
cat("warnings", run$n_warnings, "\n")
cat(strwrap(paste("approximate:", view2@approximate), width = 89), sep = "\n")
cat(sprintf("total CDR mean %s, sd %s; lifetime reserve sd %s; ratio %.2f\n", fmt(mean(cdr2)),
            fmt(psd(cdr2)), fmt(psd(total2)), psd(cdr2) / psd(total2)))
```

```text
model 2: flagged 100%, moment-matched 0, refitted 0
warnings 1
approximate: the one-year view reweights its flagged simulations only, as the light refit
of development effects (model 2) was turned off: moment matching rescues none of them. The
view is approximate, about 0.4 sd of the total claims development result off a refit per
simulation on company 337; leave light_refit at its default to refit them with a shorter
sampler (within about 0.03 sd there, at about 20 times the run time of reweighting only),
or refit (with max_refits as a budget) for the fit's own sampler
total CDR mean 103, sd 11,379; lifetime reserve sd 13,729; ratio 0.83
```

Every simulation is flagged and reweighted only. The view reports this in
`view2@approximate` and in a warning. Its CDR sd is 0.83 of the lifetime sd (0.82 in
the study, 0.78 to 0.84 over three seeds). Use it as an approximation good to
about 0.4 sds, not as a value of refit quality.

The R package's own run on Windows gives a ratio of 0.80 (CDR sd 11,401,
lifetime sd 14,261).

## 10. Several triangles and the backtest

`compartmental_segments()` fits segments on their own seeds, independent or
rank-correlated. `compartmental_one_year_segments()` does the same for the
one-year view. `compartmental_candidate()` puts the model in
`diagonal_backtest()` next to the other Bayesian models.
`compartmental_outstanding_backtest()` scores the held-out outstanding
diagonals as well as the paid diagonals.
